events.address: 121 E. Cameron Avenue, Chapel Hill, NC
events.description:
Art and Art History

Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering

August 20-October 15, 2026

Reception: August 20, 5-7 pm

 

Drawn together in graduate school by their mutual love of experimentation and play, Michelle Inez Hinojosa and Barbara Pearsall have built a collaborative practice around analogue animation and vibrant abstraction. Together, their work explores optical toys, immersive installations, and movement. Under the Tent: Whirling & Flickering features kaleidoscopic imagery, flickering abstractions, projection mapping, a hidden trapdoor, and hand-cranked wheels that transform what viewers see. After searching for the perfect venue, they are thrilled to bring their collaborative installation to UNC. Their first public artwork, Turnabout Folly, will debut in Lansing, Michigan in Fall 2026.

 

Michelle Hinojosa works at the intersection of painting, poetry, and fiber art, where she considers memory, intergenerational trauma, and migration. Born in central Texas, by way of the fields of California and Northern Mexico, Michelle uplifts traditions of making that have provided much-needed stability to a family displaced. Michelle Hinojosa is an Assistant Professor of Art at Pennsylvania State University.

 

Barbara Pearsall is an artist and educator based in Michigan. Her art practice is attentive to how deviation from material conventions can subvert or metamorphose the role of institutions, where her philosophical and political concerns manifest through material explorations of the built environment. Her pieces seek to create illusory and unusual architectural conditions as a form of resistance, interrupting real-world functionality to allow for alternative systems of order. She is an Assistant Professor of Foundations & Sculpture at Michigan State University.

 

Admission: Free

Gallery Hours: Monday-Friday, 8 am-5 pm

events.name: Before We Knew Better Art Exhibition
events.description:
The Before We Knew Better art exhibition brings together the work of Lamar Whidbee and Chris Facey to reflect on joy, memory and the experiences that shape us early in life. The exhibition looks to childhood as a place of imagination, play and connection. Rather than seeing nostalgia as a way to escape the present, the exhibition considers how memories of joy can remind us of what still matters. Whidbee and Facey ask what we carry with us from those early years and how those experiences continue to influence our well-being, relationships and sense of self. At a time when conversations around mental health are increasingly important, the exhibition offers space to pause, reflect and reconnect with the moments that first taught us about joy. 

The exhibition will be available for viewing in the art gallery at the African American Cultural Center on weekdays from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. between Aug. 17 and Sept. 25. Whidbee and Facey will discuss the exhibition during an artist talk event that will be held in the center's art gallery at 6:30 p.m. Sept. 2.

events.name: On the Ground with Ebola in DRC: Implications for Global Health and Chapel Hill
events.description:
Three months after Ebola was first declared in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), the outbreak continues to expand, with cases and deaths rising across the region. What began in the Mongbwalu health zone of Ituri Province spread to 53 health zones spanning Ituri, North Kivu, Haut-Uele and Tshopo provinces, becoming the largest Ebola outbreak in the country’s history and the second largest ever recorded worldwide.

 

William “Billy” Fischer II, MD, director of emerging pathogens for the Institute for Global Health and Infectious Diseases, and an associate professor of medicine in the division of pulmonary and critical care medicine, deployed to the outbreak in June, through the World Health Organization. He recently returned, by way of travel to Germany with an infected patient, followed by a quarantine in Switzerland.

 

In this special lecture, Dr. Fischer will share insights from his work on the front lines, with an update on the current state of preparedness and control efforts. Through years of collaboration on outbreak preparedness and response, Dr. Fischer, with Dr. David Wohl, are strengthening UNC Health’s readiness to respond to emerging threats should a disease outbreak ever occur.

events.name: On Afro-Asian Radicalism
events.description:
The complex strand of Black radical thought found in Japan pulsates with dynamism that can move in different directions. This talk suggests how to relate to this object of knowledge, or Afro-Asian radicalism. I see this task as an exercise in probing a deep well of commitment suffused with political defeats but also yearning to learn, evolve, and advance found within the intervening space between Black radicalism and Japanese intellectual and creative activities in the twentieth century. 

In Japanese, an interstice is defined as ma (間). Attunement toward such a point of entanglement is of utmost importance to Afro-Asian radicalism. The details will be culled from Black Radical Thought in Japan (University of Washington Press, 2026), which delineates Japanese intellectuals' commitment to Black struggle cultivated through the study and translation of Black texts, many connected to the midcentury U.S. Left.

About the speaker:
Yuichiro Onishi is a scholar of African American intellectual history, who locates himself in the field of Afro-Asian studies. He also continues to investigate the genesis of occupied Okinawa. He began his academic career in the Center for Ethnic Studies at the Borough of Manhattan Community College of The City University of New York (CUNY). His most recent book, Black Radical Thought in Japan: An Afro-Asian Intellectual History (University of Washington Press), was published in July 2026.

Professor Onishi's research specialties include: Black radicalism and internationalism; African American intellectual history; Asian American studies; and transnational American studies. He is an associate professor of African American and African Studies in the College of Liberal Arts at the University of Minnesota. Other departmental affiliations include: Asian American Studies; Race, Indigeneity, Disability, Gender & Sexuality Studies; American Studies; Asian & Middle Eastern Studies; Heritage Studies and Public History Graduate Program. He is also the faculty director of UMN's Liberal Arts Engagement Hub.

events.name: Hanes Visiting Artist Lecture Series: Jes Fan
events.description:
Department of Art and Art History

 

Jes Fan’s interdisciplinary practice explores the intersection of biology and identity, incorporating living matter, as well as invisible substances like melanin and hormones, that shape how we experience the world into their sculptures. Through this process, Fan looks at how these highly politicized materials form our understanding of the social constructs of race and gender, and the absurd pursuit of delimiting these as quantifiable amounts of material. Originally trained in glassmaking, Fan combines hand-blown cellular glass forms with casts made from sections of human bodies, in aqua resin and bearing uncanny flesh-like tones. Removed from the context of the figure, these forms take on abstract qualities, repeated and distorted across architectural armatures, suggesting an experience of the body increasingly intertwined with and mediated by technology. 

 

Jes Fan lives and works in Brooklyn and Hong Kong. Fan's recent solo exhibition Unbounded was at Yale University Art Gallery, New Haven, in 2026. In 2024, Andrew Kreps Gallery presented Sites of Wounding: Interchapter, Fan's first solo exhibition in New York. The same year, Fan was included in the 2024 Whitney Biennial and Greater Art Toronto. In 2023, Sites of Wounding: Chapter 2 was on view at the M+ Museum in Hong Kong for the 2023 Sigg Prize exhibition. In 2022, Fan participated in The Milk of Dreams, the 59th International Art Exhibition of La Biennale di Venezia curated by Cecilia Alemani, Venice. Fan’s work has been included in numerous group exhibitions: including Scientia Sexualis, at the Institute of Contemporary Art, Los Angeles, 2025; Symbionts: Contemporary Artists and the Biosphere, MIT List Visual Arts Center, 2022; Breaking Water, Contemporary Arts Center, Cincinnati, 2022; Soft Water Hard Stone, The Fifth New Museum Triennial, New Museum, New York, 2021; The Stomach and the Port, Liverpool Biennale, United Kingdom, 2021; NIRIN, Biennale of Sydney, Australia, 2020; The Socrates Annual 2019, Socrates Sculpture Park, Queens, 2019. Fan was awarded a Pollock-Krasner Grant in 2022.

 

An endowment established in 1983 through the generosity of Nancy and Robin Hanes supports the Art Department's Visiting Artist Series. This important program brings both established and emerging artists to campus to discuss their work in public lectures and to offer individual critiques to our M.F.A. students.  The Hanes Visiting Artist series greatly enriches both our academic programs and our outreach to the wider community.  All lectures are free and open to the public.

John “Lakota John” Locklear is a living representation of the musical cultures of southeastern North Carolina. He is a member of the Lumbee Tribe that combines the blues with the indigenous music of his ancestors. Locklear first picked up the harmonica at age 7, then the guitar. At age 10, intrigued by the sound of the slide guitar, he bought a glass slide, placed it on his pinky finger and has been sliding ever since. Mama Tonya, Papa John and Sister Layla join him to form a proud Lumbee Nation family of talented musicians.

In connection with this event, please visit these Gregg Museum exhibitions: Stories Told by Breath: Native American Voices in North Carolina and A Creek in Carolina: Artworks by Bobby C. Martin. They will be on display through Sept. 26.

events.name: Whack Attack Invasive Plant Removal Workday
events.venue: Lower Haw River State Natural Area
events.description:
Friends of Lower Haw is having an invasive plant removal workday with NC State Parks biologists on September 9th from 9:30 am until 3:00 pm, or whenever you need to leave. Meeting location is the parking lot at 4551 US Hwy 15-501 N, Pittsboro. Meet in the parking lot at 9:30 am and stay however long you want to help. We will be working in the Pegg Tract area of the Lower Haw River State Natural Area, located upstream of the Bynum Dam by US Hwy 15-501. Invasive plant workdays involve identifying and removing non-native plants using clippers, pruners, saws, and other non-motorized hand tools. Learn about invasive plants and removal techniques. Hand tools will be available, or volunteers can bring their own loppers or hand pruners.  Bring your own work gloves, insect repellent, and drinking water. Long pants, long sleeve shirt, and closed toe shoes are recommended. There are no restroom facilities at this location. Youth volunteers under age 18 are welcome to participate with signed parental consent form.

Based on new regulations, volunteers who may be interested in applying herbicide are now required to watch the new NCDA required training video (34 minutes) for non-licensed pesticide applicators before attending the workday.  You can still volunteer if you are not interested in applying herbicide and will not need to watch the training video.

events.name: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage
events.description: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.

events.name: Welcome Back to Campus: Reception for “Against Nature"
events.address: 101 S Columbia Street, Chapel Hill, NC
events.description:
The Ackland welcomes back faculty, students, and staff to campus with a celebration for its newest installation in the ART& space, Phaan Howng: Against Nature.  
In Against Nature, artist Phaan Howng positions an ornate botanical composition above wainscotting that suggests the architecture of a late nineteenth-century study or parlor. The paneling’s mint green tint evokes the green interior paints used in that period, achieved through harmful additions of arsenic. Above the wainscotting, painted vinyl banners depict a jungle of barely contained foliage with spikes and fronds of neon reds, electric oranges, cerulean blues, and bruised purples. 
During the evening, we will be celebrating with non-alcoholic drinks and snacks. Phaan will be present during the evening to mingle with attendees. Around 6:15 PM, she will briefly introduce the artwork and answer any questions. 
Join us for an evening honoring Phaan and welcoming the installation to our community, as well as starting off the semester in a fun way! 
We ask for folks to RSVP to give us a headcount for the event. No ticket purchase is required.
